name: Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome
aliases: selective vitamin B12 malabsorption with proteinuria

reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Nathan and Oski's Haematology
clinicalPearls: Consider it in a child with megaloblastic anaemia and low serum B12 who also has mild, benign proteinuria

Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CUBN (cubilin) or AMN (amnionless), which together form the cubam receptor for intrinsic factor-B12 complex in the terminal ileum
The receptor defect blocks ileal absorption of the intrinsic factor-B12 complex, causing selective B12 malabsorption
Cubilin also mediates renal tubular protein reabsorption, so tubular (low-molecular-weight) proteinuria is a characteristic feature, especially with CUBN variants
Typical onset is in infancy or early childhood with anaemia, failure to thrive, recurrent infection and sometimes neurological signs
Lifelong parenteral B12 corrects the anaemia and neurological features; the proteinuria persists but is generally benign
Intrinsic factor level and gastric parietal cell function are normal, distinguishing it from pernicious anaemia
The Schilling test historically showed malabsorption not corrected by intrinsic factor, reflecting the ileal receptor defect
reference.pathophysiology: Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome is a selective inherited defect of vitamin B12 absorption. The cubam receptor, formed by cubilin (CUBN) and amnionless (AMN), mediates endocytosis of the intrinsic factor-B12 complex at the brush border of terminal ileal enterocytes. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in either gene disable this receptor, so dietary B12 that has bound intrinsic factor cannot be taken up, producing systemic B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and, if prolonged, neurological dysfunction. Because cubilin is also expressed in the renal proximal tubule where it reclaims filtered proteins, its deficiency additionally causes low-grade tubular proteinuria. Bypassing the absorptive defect with parenteral B12 restores cobalamin status.
additionalDifferentials: Pernicious anaemia and juvenile pernicious anaemia
Other causes of childhood megaloblastic anaemia (folate deficiency)
Chronic ileal disease causing B12 malabsorption
additionalInvestigations: CUBN and AMN molecular genetic testing
Serum vitamin B12 with plasma homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
Full blood count and blood film for megaloblastic anaemia
Urinalysis and quantification of low-molecular-weight proteinuria
Intrinsic factor antibody and gastric studies to exclude pernicious anaemia
redFlags: Neurological features of B12 deficiency such as regression or subacute combined degeneration
reference.prognosis: Lifelong parenteral B12 fully corrects the anaemia and prevents neurological complications, giving an excellent outlook; the accompanying proteinuria usually remains mild and non-progressive.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis when proteinuria is dismissed as unrelated
Attributing B12 deficiency to diet or pernicious anaemia without testing absorption or genetics
Relying on oral B12, which cannot bypass the ileal receptor defect reliably
Assuming the proteinuria signifies progressive renal disease
references: GeneReviews / OMIM entries for CUBN and AMN (Imerslund-Grasbeck Syndrome)
Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Correct and prevent deficiency with lifelong parenteral hydroxocobalamin, bypassing the ileal absorptive defect
Monitor the haematological and neurological response with full blood count, serum B12, plasma homocysteine and methylmalonic acid
Follow the accompanying low-molecular-weight tubular proteinuria, which is benign and needs no specific treatment
Ensure iron and folate sufficiency to support recovery of erythropoiesis, replacing B12 before folate to avoid precipitating neurological deficit
Escalate promptly if neurological features emerge, ensuring adequate ongoing cobalamin replacement
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive CUBN or AMN disorder
